    <meta name="DC.Description" xml:lang="en" content="We propose a decentralized asset-transfer system that enjoys full privacy: no party can learn the details of a transaction, except for its issuer and its recipient. Furthermore, the recipient is not aware of the sender’s identity. Our system does not rely on consensus or synchrony assumptions, and therefore, it is responsive, since it runs at the actual network speed. Under the hood, every transaction creates a consumable coin equipped with a non-interactive zero-knowledge proof (NIZK) that confirms that the issuer has sufficient funds without revealing any information about her identity, the recipient’s identity, or the payment amount. Moreover, we equip our system with a regulatory enforcement mechanism that can be used to regulate transfer limits or restrict specific addresses from sending or receiving funds, while preserving the system’s privacy guarantees.
Finally, we report on PaxPay, our implementation of Fully Private Asset Transfer (FPAT) that uses the Gnark library for the NIZKs. In our benchmark, PaxPay exhibits better performance than earlier proposals that either ensure only partial privacy, require some kind of network synchrony or do not implement regulation features. Our system thus reconciles privacy, responsiveness, regulation enforcement and performance." >

<div class="ltx_abstract" id="abstract">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
<p class="ltx_p">We propose a decentralized asset-transfer system that enjoys <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">full privacy</em>: no party can learn the details of a transaction, except for its issuer and its recipient. Furthermore, the recipient is not aware of the sender’s identity.
Our system does not rely on consensus or synchrony assumptions, and therefore, it is <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">responsive</em>, since it runs at the actual network speed.
Under the hood, every transaction creates a consumable <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">coin</em> equipped with a non-interactive zero-knowledge proof (NIZK) that confirms that the issuer has sufficient funds without revealing any information about her identity, the recipient’s identity, or the payment amount.
Moreover, we equip our system with a <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">regulatory enforcement</em> mechanism
that can be used to regulate transfer limits or restrict specific addresses from sending or receiving funds, while preserving the system’s privacy guarantees.</p>
<p class="ltx_p">Finally, we report on <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">PaxPay</em>, our implementation of Fully Private Asset Transfer (FPAT) that uses the Gnark library for the NIZKs.
In our benchmark, PaxPay exhibits better performance than earlier proposals that either ensure only partial privacy, require some kind of network synchrony or do not implement regulation features.
Our system thus reconciles privacy, responsiveness, regulation enforcement and performance.</p>

<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<section id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1" class="ltx_subparagraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subparagraph">Payments, with and without consensus.</h4>

<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Bitcoin <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite> revolutionized the world of finance by proposing a fully decentralized asset-transfer system that allows an open set of users to consistently exchange assets without any mutual trust.
Instead of relying on a central authority, users repeatedly engage in a form of <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">consensus</em> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>, <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite> to maintain a replicated ledger – an ever-growing record of all transactions.
It was later observed <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>, <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>]</cite> that, strictly speaking, global consensus, a notoriously hard task <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>, <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite> that requires partial synchrony <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>, <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite>, is not necessary in payments.
In most common cases, when every account is maintained by a dedicated user, asset transfer can be implemented in an asynchronous, <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">responsive</em> way on top of the <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">reliable-broadcast</em> primitive <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite> (instead of consensus).</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Reliable broadcast is weaker than consensus as it allows the correct users to eventually and consistently agree on the <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">set</em> of issued transactions but not on their order.
However, it turned out to be strong enough to prevent <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">double spending</em>, a major issue in asset-transfer systems.
This observation gave rise to a series of purely asynchronous, <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">consensus-free</em> asset-transfer systems <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>, <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>, <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2" class="ltx_subparagraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subparagraph">Privacy and regulations in payment systems.</h4>

<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">However, a decentralized asset-transfer system, as any replicated service, still faces a vital challenge of preserving privacy of its users.
Indeed, in all the mentioned payment protocols, all transactions are inherently <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">public</em> and every user’s activities are traceable.
Hiding the amount of a payment offers <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">confidentiality</em> and hiding the identities of the sender and receiver offers <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">anonymity</em>. Fully <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">private</em> payment systems ought to offer both confidentiality and anonymity.

Furthermore, many important payment applications, such as Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite>, require mechanisms for <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">regulatory enforcement</em>, such as limiting transaction amounts.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Existing distributed asset-transfer systems (<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>, <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>, <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>, <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>, <a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>, <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">44</a>, <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>]</cite>, to name a few) arbitrate a trade-off between the four following aspects: <span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(a) Privacy guarantees</span>, <span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(b) Model assumptions</span>, <span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(c) Regulation enforcement</span>, and <span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(d) Performance</span>.
Reconciling these four aspects is a onerous challenge, as strengthening one aspect often weakens another.
Table <a href="#S1.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Summary. ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Fast, Private and Regulated Payments in Asynchronous Networks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> provides a detailed comparison of several payment systems across these dimensions. This table and its content are detailed and discussed in Section <a href="#S8" title="8 Discussion and comparison with related protocols ‣ Fast, Private and Regulated Payments in Asynchronous Networks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx3" class="ltx_subparagraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subparagraph">FPAT and PaxPay.</h4>

<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">In this paper, we address this challenge.
We introduce the abstraction of <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Fully Private Asset Transfer</em> (FPAT) that maintains conventional safety and liveness properties of a payment system (informally, no asset is spent twice and every transaction takes effect), while at the same time making sure that no transaction’s detail is leaked to a non-involved party.
We then describe the <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">PaxPay</em> protocol, a FPAT implementation over an <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">asynchronous</em> network.
PaxPay has been implemented in Golang using Gnark library <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">As in UTXO transactions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite>, to execute a transfer, the sender <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">spends</em> a set of <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">old coins</em> it has received earlier and <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">generates</em> a set of <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">new coins</em> of the same total value.
Every coin is uniquely identified by its <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">serial number</em>.
Every coin should be signed by a sufficiently large set (a <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2/3" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">quorum</em>) of <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">validators</em>, i.e., dedicated parties that maintain lists of spent coins and make sure that no user spends a same coin twice.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">The protocol operates in an
asynchronous network, where any number of users and less than one third of validators can be <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Byzantine</em> (deviating arbitrarily from its algorithm).
The rest of the validators are considered <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">semi-honest</em> (following their algorithm but possibly sharing their states with the adversary).
To ensure that the transfer is legal, several assertions have to be checked: the total value of the spent coins equals the total value of the new coins, the user that calls the transfer is the owner of the spent coins, all the coins are properly signed, etc.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">To provide <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">full privacy</em> (confidentiality and anonymity), PaxPay leverages several cryptographic primitives.
The legality of transactions is verified within a non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs (NIZK).
A <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">blind</em> signature scheme is used at the validators’ side and these signatures are verified within the NIZK, allowing not to reveal the coins or their signatures when spending them.
To verify these signatures efficiently, we implemented the NIZK using the Groth16 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite> scheme and employed a pairing-based signature scheme <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite>.
We then selected a pair of elliptic curves that form a chain to instantiate these cryptographic primitives, allowing efficient verification of the signature within the NIZK (we refer to Section <a href="#S7" title="7 PaxPay implementation and performance ‣ Fast, Private and Regulated Payments in Asynchronous Networks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> for more details).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx4" class="ltx_subparagraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subparagraph">Regulation.</h4>

<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">We also describe and implement a regulation enforcement mechanism that can be built on top of our system.
Similar to PEReDi and PARScoin <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>, <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite>, our approach allows setting limits on individual transfer amounts or the cumulative amount transferred by a user since they joined the system.
However, regulations for CBDCs mandate stringent measures for Anti-Money Laundering (AML) and Countering the Financing of Terrorism (CFT).
These measures go beyond simply limiting transaction amounts.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">PEReDi and PARScoin <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>, <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite> address these requirements and enable validators to reveal the details of transfers if needed.
This could put at risk the privacy of the users.
Their approach relies on additional trust assumptions, requiring non-Byzantine validators to be <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">honest</em> (i.e., not to share any information with the adversary) to maintain privacy.
We avoid such extra assumptions by equipping the users with a mechanism to generate cryptographic proofs for arbitrary statements about the histories of their transactions.
It enables extracting a requested information without disclosing the full content of the transaction histories.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Additionally, we incorporate a novel mechanism, empowering the regulator to impose <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">sanctions</em>, precluding specific addresses from interactions with other users.
This ensures compliance with traditional financial sanctions emitted by the central banks or intergovernmental organizations (e.g., the UN<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span><a href="https://main.un.org/securitycouncil/en/sanctions/information" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://main.un.org/securitycouncil/en/sanctions/information</a></span></span></span>) and
explicitly required by the European Central Bank for the digital Euro <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">The regulatory mechanism is implemented by introducing an additional type of coin, referred to as the <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">compliance coin</em>.
At a time, each user may possess several
regular coins, but only one
unique compliance coin.
In each transfer, the compliance coin of the sender must be spent together with the regular coins.
Then a new
compliance coin containing the information of the transfer is generated (i.e., signed by a quorum of validators).
The compliance coin thus allows us to keep track records of all the interactions of a user with the system, which can be seen
as a commitment to the transaction history and some aggregated values.
To generate an initially valid compliance coin, before joining the system, the user must be registered with a <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">regulatory authority</em>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx4.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Our regulation framework incurs very low impact on the transaction throughput.
It mainly affects the transaction proving time (by doubling it compared to the non-regulated case), which we do not consider a primary performance factor.
In contrast, such a mechanism could be difficult and performance-intensive to implement in other protocols that rely on Sigma protocols <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>]</cite>, such as UTT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>]</cite>, Zef <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>, Peredi <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>]</cite>, and Parscoin <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite>, which use these protocols to construct their NIZKs.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx5" class="ltx_subparagraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subparagraph">Performance.</h4>

<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Finally, we evaluated the performance of PaxPay, in comparison with state-of-the-art payment systems that provide privacy-preserving and/or regulatory-enforcement features (cf Table <a href="#S1.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Summary. ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Fast, Private and Regulated Payments in Asynchronous Networks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>).
In our benchmark (detailed in Section <a href="#S7.SS2" title="7.2 Performance analysis ‣ 7 PaxPay implementation and performance ‣ Fast, Private and Regulated Payments in Asynchronous Networks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7.2</span></a>), we witness that
PaxPay can process at least <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="8" display="inline"><mn>8</mn></math> times more transactions per second than any of these systems.
The benchmark on AWS EC2 instances demonstrates a throughput of <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="925" display="inline"><mn>925</mn></math> transactions per second.
The performance gains can be explained by the use of Groth16 as a succinct NIZK with low verification cost.
In return, this comes at the cost of heavy computations required to generate a proof.
The time required to create a transfer request with limited computational resources in PaxPay on a one-core CPU is up to <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="7s" display="inline"><mrow><mn>7</mn><mo>⁢</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> for example.
However, given the throughput gains, this appears to be a good trade-off.
Moreover, PaxPay’s design allows for pushing the throughput even further by parallelizing the validator’s load on several machines.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx6" class="ltx_subparagraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subparagraph">Full version.</h4>

<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">The full version of this paper <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite> incorporates more details including the algorithms that implement PaxPay, the security proofs, the link toward PaxPay implementation and additional details on the benchmarks.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx7" class="ltx_subparagraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subparagraph">Summary.</h4>

<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">To sum up our contributions:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="S1.I1.i1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\blacksquare" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="normal">■</mi></math></span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">We formalize the problem by introducing the <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Fully Private Asset Transfer</em> abstraction (FPAT).</p>
</div>
</li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="S1.I1.i2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\blacksquare" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="normal">■</mi></math></span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">We propose PaxPay, a protocol that implements a FPAT object, and prove its correctness.</p>
</div>
</li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="S1.I1.i3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\blacksquare" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="normal">■</mi></math></span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">We implement PaxPay in Golang, mainly leveraging on the Gnark <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite> library.</p>
</div>
</li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="S1.I1.i4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\blacksquare" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="normal">■</mi></math></span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">PaxPay achieves a true reconciliation of <span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(a) Privacy</span>, <span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(b) Model Assumptions</span> (network synchrony and trust assumptions for validators), <span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(c) Regulation Enforcement</span>, and <span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(d) Performance</span>.
Unlike earlier works that propose trade-offs, PaxPay excels in each of these aspects simultaneously, bringing together the best of all these dimensions:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1.i4.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">–</span></span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Regarding <span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Privacy</span>, transactions in PaxPay are <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">confidential</em>, <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">fully anonymous</em>, and <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">unlinkable</em>, ensuring the most robust privacy guarantees.</p>
</div>
</li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">–</span></span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Regarding <span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Model Assumptions</span>, the system tolerates up to one-third Byzantine validators, with the remaining validators only required to be <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">semi-honest</em>, and does not rely on the network synchrony.</p>
</div>
</li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">–</span></span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Regarding <span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Regulation</span>, PaxPay provides a comprehensive regulation framework by enabling users to generate cryptographic proofs about their transaction history, setting spending limits, and incorporating a sanction mechanism preventing sanctioned addresses to receive or spend funds.</p>
</div>
</li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">–</span></span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Finally, our implementation outperforms
state-of-the-art protocols.
Also, we show that the transaction throughput of PaxPay scales with the computational power of validators.
The system can further increase its supported throughput by distributing validators across additional machines.</p>
</div>
</li>
</ul>
</div>
</li>
<li id="S1.I1.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="S1.I1.i5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\blacksquare" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="normal">■</mi></math></span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">PaxPay can find a variety of use cases such as a standalone payment system, a <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">layer 2</em> solution on top of a blockchain (brings scalability, compliance, or privacy) or a CBDC.</p>
</div>
</li>
</ul>

<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related work</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">We overview payment systems related to our work, the summary of our comparative analysis is presented in Table <a href="#S1.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Summary. ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Fast, Private and Regulated Payments in Asynchronous Networks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> compares this work with the related works. Additional details about the comparison can be found in the full version of the paper.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1" class="ltx_subparagraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subparagraph">Consensus-free payment systems.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Gupta <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite> and Guerraoui <span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">et al.</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>]</cite> proposed a payment system that replaces the conventional consensus-based synchronization with the secure broadcast primitive <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>, <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>]</cite>.
Systems like Astro <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite>, FastPay <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>]</cite>, Zef <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>, PARScoin <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite> and UTT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>]</cite> extend this approach, operating without consensus in asynchronous networks.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2" class="ltx_subparagraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subparagraph">Private payment systems without regulation.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Zerocash <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite>, Zexe <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite>, Monero <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite>, Quisqus <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite> and Lelantus <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>]</cite> are payment systems built on top of blockchains and consensus.
They provide <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">privacy</em> via NIZKs or ring signatures.
Zerocash and Zexe <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>, <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite> use <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">commitments</em> stored in Merkle trees and nullifiers to prevent double spending. Each transaction is accompanied by an NIZK to provide privacy but these systems offer inherently low transaction throughput.
Monero <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite> and Quisquis <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite> relies on ring signatures to provide anonymity but only limits the sender and receiver’s identity to a small subset of the users, known as the <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">anonymity set</em>.
Compared to Monero, Quisquis offers stronger privacy guarantees in certain scenarios preventing possible de-anonymization.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Lelantus <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>, <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite> offers privacy via NIZK requires less advanced cryptographic assumptions than Zerocash or Zexe, for instance it does not require any trusted setup. It also proposes batch verification for validators.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">All payment systems mentioned so far are built on a blockchain and, thus, require consensus.
Baudet et al. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite> describe Zef, a private payment system, that assumes an asynchronous network but only provides <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">partial</em> anonymity and confidentiality.
To improve performance, the transaction data in Zef is distributed over a set of <span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">authorities</span>.
Each authority can be sharded – i.e., distributed over several machines, as in Astro <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite> and in this work.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx3" class="ltx_subparagraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subparagraph">Private payment systems with regulation.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">PRCash <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">44</a>]</cite>, Platypus <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>]</cite>, PEReDi <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>]</cite>, PARScoin <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite> and UTT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>]</cite> incorporate certain regulatory features into private payment systems.
A common element in their designs is the reliance on NIZK.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Garman et al. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite> were among the first to address regulation by enforcing <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">policies</em> such as fixing a spending limit on a system with a similar construction as Zerocash.
Their system has not been implemented and, as it is built on top of Zerocash, it shares the same major drawbacks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">PRCash <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">44</a>]</cite>, as Zerocash, is blockchain-based and operates with commitments but offers only partial privacy.
Regulation features proposed by PRCash are limited: users cannot spend more than a predefined amount set by the regulator within a certain time window.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">UTT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>]</cite>, a concurrent work to our paper, proposes an asynchronous private payment system with privacy guarantees,
a low transaction latency and a high transaction throughput.
Both UTT and PaxPay protocols follow a similar approach, using coin commitments and consistent broadcast to create and spend coins in a fully private manner.
However, the regulation features offered by UTT are restricted to
the <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">anonymity budget</em> that limits the amount of anonymous coins that a user can transfer.
Compared to UTT, PaxPay offers a more comprehensive set of regulation features and exhibit better performance, due to improved NIZK construction.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Platypus <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>]</cite> offers regulation features of holding limits, receiving limits, and spending limits.
It uses NIZK with low verification costs to increase transaction throughput.
However, unlike other payment systems described in this section, Platypus is a centralized payment system rather than a distributed one.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">PEReDi <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>]</cite> is an account-based system.
The regulation framework enforces spending and receiving limits for each transaction and imposes restrictions on the maximum amount a user can hold.
Additionally, the system allows validators to trace funds and reveal details of certain payments.
Users encrypt their transaction details with a threshold encryption scheme so that a quorum of validators can decrypt them.
PEReDi needs a synchronous network and <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">correct</em> (<span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">i.e.</span>, non-Byzantine) validators must be <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">honest</em> (<span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">i.e.</span>, strictly follow the protocol and avoid seeking additional information).
In contrast, most systems discussed here (as well as ours) are designed to tolerate <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">semi-honest</em> correct validators.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Concurrently with this work, the same authors have recently proposed PARScoin <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite>.
PARScoin enhances PEReDi by allowing asynchronous transactions yet still requires honest validators and faces limited throughput.
PARScoin’s protocol is similar to the one employed by UTT and our work, relying on Byzantine consistent broadcast.
Our work differs from PARScoin in the NIZK construction which offers better performance, fewer assumptions on the validators and additional regulations features.
Also, neither PRCash, PARScoin nor PEReDi have conducted latency tests to evaluate the maximum transaction throughput of their systems, they only provide benchmarks of their primitives (such as the time to prove or verify a transaction).</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Other decentralised privacy-preserving payment systems adopt this auditability approach such as <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>, <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx4" class="ltx_subparagraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subparagraph">Specifications for a responsive and private payment system.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">In this paper, we introduce a new specification (inspired by the formalism recently proposed by Albouy et al. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>), as existing ones do not address our particular problem.
They describe either private payment systems that cannot be implemented in asynchronous networks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>,
asynchronous payment systems that lack anonymity <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>, <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>, <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>]</cite>, or non-sequential specifications that do not align with how specifications are typically defined in the distributed systems literature <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>, <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>, <a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Model</h2>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Participants and adversary</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">The system is composed of two types of participants:</p>
<ul id="S3.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="S3.I1.i1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\blacksquare" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="normal">■</mi></math></span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">A set <math id="S3.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{U}" display="inline"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒰</mi></math> of <math id="S3.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U" display="inline"><mi>U</mi></math> <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">users</em> of the payment system.</p>
</div>
</li>
<li id="S3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="S3.I1.i2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\blacksquare" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="normal">■</mi></math></span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">A set <math id="S3.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{V}" display="inline"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi></math> of <math id="S3.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N=3f+1" display="inline"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>⁢</mo><mi>f</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></math> <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">validators</em>.</p>
</div>
</li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Here <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline"><mi>f</mi></math> denotes the maximum number of validators that can go <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Byzantine</em>, i.e., deviate from the protocol.
A non-Byzantine (faithful following the protocol) is called <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">correct</em>.
Correct validators may, however, be <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">semi-honest</em> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite>: a correct party may try to learn as much as possible from the messages they receive from other parties, which may involve colluding and pooling their views together.
In contrast, <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">honest</em> validators that are not trying to learn any information.
The correct participants are thus following the protocol but they may exchange information with any other participant (Byzantine or not) to learn as much as possible.
As we shall see, Byzantine participants pose challenges to all correctness aspects of our system (safety, liveness and privacy),
while semi-honest participants affect only privacy.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">The adversary <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{A}" display="inline"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi></math> thus controls any number of users and all validators, but at most <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline"><mi>f</mi></math> validators can deviate from the protocol.
<math id="S3.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{A}" display="inline"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi></math> can be seen as a hybrid adversary between honest and semi-honest.
We assume that <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{A}" display="inline"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi></math> is <span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">static</span> and <span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">network-ignorant</span>: the set of Byzantine participants controlled by <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{A}" display="inline"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi></math> is chosen a priori, and <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{A}" display="inline"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi></math> has no information about message delay between the validators and the other participants.
It can delay the messages but must eventually deliver them.
Conventionally, the adversary <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{A}" display="inline"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi></math> is computationally bounded.
More precisely, <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{A}" display="inline"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi></math> is <span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">probabilistic polynomial-time</span> (PPT).</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Every participant is provided with a pair of distinct public and secret addresses denoted <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="apk" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> and <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="ask" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>.
These addresses are used to identify users and validators.
The public addresses of the validators are known to every participant.
Otherwise, a user only needs to know the identifiers of the users she engages in transfers with.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Network and communications</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Concerning the network, we assume <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">asynchronous</em> but <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">reliable</em> communication.
The participants can communicate via <span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">anonymous</span>, <span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">secure</span>, and <span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">asynchronous</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">network channels</span>.
The channels do not modify or create messages.
If a correct participants sends a message to a correct one, the message is eventually received, though we assume no bounds on the communication delays.
The sender’s identity is not known to the receiver, but the receiver can still respond to the sender.
No other participant can tell who is the sender or the receiver, or tamper with the message content. We could use a network based on Syverson et al. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>]</cite> work.
We consider that the latency distribution is the same for all the channels.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Cryptographic tools</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Our protocol makes use of several cryptographic tools that we list below.
Due to the space constraints, we only give informal definitions and refer to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite> for more details.
Also, in the algorithms mentioned below, we omit the security parameters taken as inputs.
Some primitives require a setup phase, which will be handled by a trusted third party <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{T}" display="inline"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi></math>.
Note that these setups could be carried out via MPC <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite> between the validators.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx1" class="ltx_subparagraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subparagraph">
<math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(k,N)" display="inline"><mrow><mo class="ltx_mathvariant_bold" mathvariant="bold" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝒌</mi><mo class="ltx_mathvariant_bold" mathvariant="bold">,</mo><mi>𝑵</mi><mo class="ltx_mathvariant_bold" mathvariant="bold" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>-Threshold Blind Signature Scheme.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Tuple of algorithms <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\Pi_{\mathsf{sig}}\mathsf{=(SETUP_{Sig},}" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Π</mi><mi>𝗌𝗂𝗀</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝖲𝖤𝖳𝖴𝖯</mi><mi>𝖲𝗂𝗀</mi></msub><mo>,</mo></mrow></mrow></math> <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathsf{BLIND,SIGN,UNBLIND,AGGREGATE,VERIFY_{Sig})}" display="inline"><mrow><mi>𝖡𝖫𝖨𝖭𝖣</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝖲𝖨𝖦𝖭</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝖴𝖭𝖡𝖫𝖨𝖭𝖣</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝖠𝖦𝖦𝖱𝖤𝖦𝖠𝖳𝖤</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝖵𝖤𝖱𝖨𝖥𝖸</mi><mi>𝖲𝗂𝗀</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> allowing to divide a secret key <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="sk" display="inline"><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> in <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math> fragments <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[sk_{i}]_{i=1}^{N}" display="inline"><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>⁢</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup></math> between <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math> signers, such that valid signatures from any subset of <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline"><mi>k</mi></math> signers can be aggregated into a valid signature on behalf of the corresponding public key <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="pk_{agg}" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁢</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>.
Each fragment <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="sk_{i}" display="inline"><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>⁢</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> has a corresponding public key <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="pk_{i}" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁢</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> so that a partial signature <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{i}" display="inline"><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> generated with <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="sk_{i}" display="inline"><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>⁢</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> can be verified with respect to <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="pk_{i}" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁢</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>.
Moreover, the signers sign a blinding version <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{m}" display="inline"><mover accent="true"><mi>m</mi><mo>~</mo></mover></math> of a message <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline"><mi>m</mi></math> such that no information on <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline"><mi>m</mi></math> can be derived from <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{m}" display="inline"><mover accent="true"><mi>m</mi><mo>~</mo></mover></math>.
A valid signature with respect to <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{m}" display="inline"><mi>m</mi></math> can then be computed.
Signature are unforgeable, which means that no PPT adversary can forge a valid partial signature <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{i}" display="inline"><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> of a message <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline"><mi>m</mi></math> that correctly verifies against <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="pk_{i}" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁢</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> without the knowledge of <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m22" class="ltx_Math" alttext="sk_{i}" display="inline"><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>⁢</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>.
As a blind signature, this should not also be possible for a signer to eventually make the link between the signature is has issued, and the final signature (after <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m23" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathsf{UNBLIND}" display="inline"><mi>𝖴𝖭𝖡𝖫𝖨𝖭𝖣</mi></math> and <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m24" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathsf{AGGREGATE}" display="inline"><mi>𝖠𝖦𝖦𝖱𝖤𝖦𝖠𝖳𝖤</mi></math>).</p>
<ul id="S3.I2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S3.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="S3.I2.i1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\blacksquare" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="normal">■</mi></math></span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p"><math id="S3.I2.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathsf{SETUP_{Sig}}(k,N)\rightarrow([sk_{i}]_{i=1}^{N},[pk_{i}]_{i=1}^{N},pk_%
{agg})" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝖲𝖤𝖳𝖴𝖯</mi><mi>𝖲𝗂𝗀</mi></msub><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>⁢</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁢</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁢</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>: Randomized algorithm run by a trusted party. Takes as input threshold parameters <math id="S3.I2.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(k,N)" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and returns a list of <math id="S3.I2.i1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline"><mi>N</mi></math> signing keys <math id="S3.I2.i1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[sk_{i}]_{i=1}^{N}" display="inline"><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>⁢</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup></math> and one corresponding verification key <math id="S3.I2.i1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="pk_{agg}" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁢</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>.</p>
</div>
</li>
<li id="S3.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="S3.I2.i2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\blacksquare" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="normal">■</mi></math></span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p"><math id="S3.I2.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathsf{BLIND}(m,b)\rightarrow(\tilde{m})" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>𝖡𝖫𝖨𝖭𝖣</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>m</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>: Takes as input a message <math id="S3.I2.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline"><mi>m</mi></math> and a blinding factor <math id="S3.I2.i2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline"><mi>b</mi></math>, returns a blinded message <math id="S3.I2.i2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{m}" display="inline"><mover accent="true"><mi>m</mi><mo>~</mo></mover></math>.</p>
</div>
</li>
<li id="S3.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="S3.I2.i3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\blacksquare" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="normal">■</mi></math></span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p"><math id="S3.I2.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathsf{SIGN}(\tilde{m},sk_{i})\rightarrow\tilde{\sigma_{i}}" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>𝖲𝖨𝖦𝖭</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>m</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>⁢</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mover accent="true"><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>~</mo></mover></mrow></math>: Takes as input a blinded message <math id="S3.I2.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{m}" display="inline"><mover accent="true"><mi>m</mi><mo>~</mo></mover></math> and a secret key <math id="S3.I2.i3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="sk_{i}" display="inline"><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>⁢</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>, and returns a partial blinded signature <math id="S3.I2.i3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\sigma_{i}}" display="inline"><mover accent="true"><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>~</mo></mover></math>.</p>
</div>
</li>
<li id="S3.I2.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="S3.I2.i4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\blacksquare" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="normal">■</mi></math></span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p"><math id="S3.I2.i4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathsf{UNBLIND}(\tilde{m},\tilde{\sigma}_{i},b)\rightarrow\sigma_{i}" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>𝖴𝖭𝖡𝖫𝖨𝖭𝖣</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>m</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>σ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>: Takes as input a blinded message <math id="S3.I2.i4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{m}" display="inline"><mover accent="true"><mi>m</mi><mo>~</mo></mover></math>, the blinding factor <math id="S3.I2.i4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline"><mi>b</mi></math> used to blind <math id="S3.I2.i4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline"><mi>m</mi></math> and the corresponding partial blinded signature <math id="S3.I2.i4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\sigma_{i}}" display="inline"><mover accent="true"><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>~</mo></mover></math>, and returns a valid partial signature <math id="S3.I2.i4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{i}" display="inline"><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> for the original message <math id="S3.I2.i4.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathsf{m}" display="inline"><mi>𝗆</mi></math>.</p>
</div>
</li>
<li id="S3.I2.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="S3.I2.i5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\blacksquare" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="normal">■</mi></math></span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p"><math id="S3.I2.i5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathsf{AGGREGATE}([\sigma_{i}]_{i=1}^{k})\rightarrow\sigma" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>𝖠𝖦𝖦𝖱𝖤𝖦𝖠𝖳𝖤</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>σ</mi></mrow></math>: Takes as input a list of <math id="S3.I2.i5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline"><mi>k</mi></math> signatures <math id="S3.I2.i5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[\sigma_{i}]_{i=1}^{k}" display="inline"><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math> and produce a signature <math id="S3.I2.i5.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline"><mi>σ</mi></math> such that <math id="S3.I2.i5.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline"><mi>σ</mi></math> is a valid signature on behalf of the public key <math id="S3.I2.i5.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="pk_{agg}" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁢</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> if and only if all <math id="S3.I2.i5.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{i}" display="inline"><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> are valid signatures for distinct public keys <math id="S3.I2.i5.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="pk_{i}" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁢</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>.</p>
</div>
</li>
<li id="S3.I2.i6" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="S3.I2.i6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\blacksquare" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="normal">■</mi></math></span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p"><math id="S3.I2.i6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathsf{VERIFY_{Sig}}(m,\sigma,pk)\rightarrow b" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝖵𝖤𝖱𝖨𝖥𝖸</mi><mi>𝖲𝗂𝗀</mi></msub><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>σ</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>: Takes as input a partial or aggregated signature <math id="S3.I2.i6.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline"><mi>σ</mi></math> of a message <math id="S3.I2.i6.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline"><mi>m</mi></math> and returns a bit <math id="S3.I2.i6.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline"><mi>b</mi></math> of value <math id="S3.I2.i6.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline"><mn>1</mn></math> if <math id="S3.I2.i6.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline"><mi>σ</mi></math> is valid with respect to <math id="S3.I2.i6.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="pk" display="inline"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> and <math id="S3.I2.i6.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline"><mn>0</mn></math> otherwise. The signature can be a partial or aggregated signature.</p>
</div>
</li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx2" class="ltx_subparagraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subparagraph">
<span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Collision-Resistant</span> and <span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Preimage-Resistant</span> Pseudorandom Function Family <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite>.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">A family of functions <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathsf{PRF}=\{\mathsf{PRF}_{s}:\{0,1\}^{*}\rightarrow\{0,1\}^{O(|s|)}\}_{s}" display="inline"><mrow><mi>𝖯𝖱𝖥</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>𝖯𝖱𝖥</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow></math>, where <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline"><mi>s</mi></math> denotes a seed, computationally indistinguishable from a random function family.
<span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Collision-Resistance</span> means here that it is computationally infeasible to find couples <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(s,x)\neq(s^{\prime},x^{\prime})" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>≠</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> such that <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathsf{PRF}_{s}(x)=\mathsf{PRF}_{s^{\prime}}(x^{\prime})" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝖯𝖱𝖥</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝖯𝖱𝖥</mi><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></msub><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></math>.
<span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Preimage-Resistance</span> means that it is computationally infeasible, given <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline"><mi>y</mi></math>, to find <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(s,x)" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> such that <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathsf{PRF}_{s}(x)=y" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝖯𝖱𝖥</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx3" class="ltx_subparagraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subparagraph">Non-Interactive Zero-Knowledge Proof (NIZK) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite>.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">A tuple of algorithms <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Pi_{\mathsf{proof}}=\mathsf{(SETUP_{NIZK},PROVE,VERIFY_{NIZK})}" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Π</mi><mi>𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗈𝖿</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝖲𝖤𝖳𝖴𝖯</mi><mi>𝖭𝖨𝖹𝖪</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>𝖯𝖱𝖮𝖵𝖤</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝖵𝖤𝖱𝖨𝖥𝖸</mi><mi>𝖭𝖨𝖹𝖪</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> allowing a <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">prover</em> to prove to a <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">verifier</em> that, given a statement defined by an NP relation <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{R}(a,b)" display="inline"><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and an instance <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathsf{public\_input}" display="inline"><mrow><mi>𝗉𝗎𝖻𝗅𝗂𝖼</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">_</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mi>𝗂𝗇𝗉𝗎𝗍</mi></mrow></math>, she knows a witness <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathsf{private\_input}" display="inline"><mrow><mi>𝗉𝗋𝗂𝗏𝖺𝗍𝖾</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">_</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mi>𝗂𝗇𝗉𝗎𝗍</mi></mrow></math> such that <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{R}(\mathsf{public\_input},\mathsf{private\_input})" display="inline"><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>𝗉𝗎𝖻𝗅𝗂𝖼</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">_</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mi>𝗂𝗇𝗉𝗎𝗍</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>𝗉𝗋𝗂𝗏𝖺𝗍𝖾</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">_</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mi>𝗂𝗇𝗉𝗎𝗍</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.</p>
<ul id="S3.I3" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S3.I3.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="S3.I3.i1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\blacksquare" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="normal">■</mi></math></span> 
<div id="S3.I3.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p"><math id="S3.I3.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathsf{SETUP_{NIZK}(}\mathcal{R})\rightarrow\mathsf{pp_{NIZK}}" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝖲𝖤𝖳𝖴𝖯</mi><mi>𝖭𝖨𝖹𝖪</mi></msub><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msub><mi>𝗉𝗉</mi><mi>𝖭𝖨𝖹𝖪</mi></msub></mrow></math>: Randomised algorithm run by a trusted party. Takes as input a relation <math id="S3.I3.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{R}" display="inline"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi></math> and outputs public parameters <math id="S3.I3.i1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathsf{pp_{NIZK}}" display="inline"><msub><mi>𝗉𝗉</mi><mi>𝖭𝖨𝖹𝖪</mi></msub></math> (also known as common reference string). These public parameters are taken as input by the two following algorithms <math id="S3.I3.i1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathsf{PROVE}" display="inline"><mi>𝖯𝖱𝖮𝖵𝖤</mi></math> and <math id="S3.I3.i1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathsf{VERIFY}" display="inline"><mi>𝖵𝖤𝖱𝖨𝖥𝖸</mi></math>, but we omit it to lighten the notation.</p>
</div>
</li>
<li id="S3.I3.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="S3.I3.i2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\blacksquare" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="normal">■</mi></math></span> 
<div id="S3.I3.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p"><math id="S3.I3.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathsf{PROVE(\mathsf{public\_input},\mathsf{private\_input},\mathsf{pp_{NIZK}%
})\rightarrow\pi}" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>𝖯𝖱𝖮𝖵𝖤</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>𝗉𝗎𝖻𝗅𝗂𝖼</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">_</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mi>𝗂𝗇𝗉𝗎𝗍</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>𝗉𝗋𝗂𝗏𝖺𝗍𝖾</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">_</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mi>𝗂𝗇𝗉𝗎𝗍</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝗉𝗉</mi><mi>𝖭𝖨𝖹𝖪</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow></math>: Randomised algorithm. Takes as inputs instance and witness. Outputs a proof <math id="S3.I3.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline"><mi>π</mi></math> such that :</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.I3.i2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p"><math id="S3.I3.i2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{R}(\mathsf{public\_input},\mathsf{private\_input})" display="inline"><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>𝗉𝗎𝖻𝗅𝗂𝖼</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">_</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mi>𝗂𝗇𝗉𝗎𝗍</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>𝗉𝗋𝗂𝗏𝖺𝗍𝖾</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">_</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mi>𝗂𝗇𝗉𝗎𝗍</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.</p>
</div>
</li>
<li id="S3.I3.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="S3.I3.i3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\blacksquare" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="normal">■</mi></math></span> 
<div id="S3.I3.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p"><math id="S3.I3.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathsf{VERIFY_{NIZK}(\mathsf{public\_input},pp_{NIZK},\pi)\rightarrow b}" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝖵𝖤𝖱𝖨𝖥𝖸</mi><mi>𝖭𝖨𝖹𝖪</mi></msub><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>𝗉𝗎𝖻𝗅𝗂𝖼</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">_</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mi>𝗂𝗇𝗉𝗎𝗍</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝗉𝗉</mi><mi>𝖭𝖨𝖹𝖪</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>𝖻</mi></mrow></math>: Takes as input an instance <math id="S3.I3.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathsf{public\_input}" display="inline"><mrow><mi>𝗉𝗎𝖻𝗅𝗂𝖼</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">_</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mi>𝗂𝗇𝗉𝗎𝗍</mi></mrow></math> and a proof <math id="S3.I3.i3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline"><mi>π</mi></math>. Outputs <math id="S3.I3.i3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline"><mn>1</mn></math> if the proof is valid and <math id="S3.I3.i3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline"><mn>0</mn></math> otherwise.</p>
</div>
</li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx4" class="ltx_subparagraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subparagraph">Incremental commitment scheme.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">A tuple of algorithms <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Pi_{com}=(\mathsf{COM},\mathsf{INCR})" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Π</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mi>o</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝖢𝖮𝖬</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝖨𝖭𝖢𝖱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> that allows us, given a sequence of messages <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[m_{i}]_{i=1}^{n}" display="inline"><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup></math> and a sequence of randomness <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[r_{i}]_{i=1}^{n}" display="inline"><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup></math>, to produce a <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">commitment</em> <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math>.
The commitment is <span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">hiding</span>, i.e., no information on <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[m_{i}]_{i=1}^{n}" display="inline"><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup></math> can be derived from <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math> without prior knowledge on <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx4.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[r_{i}]_{i=1}^{n}" display="inline"><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup></math>.
The commitment is also <span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">binding</span>, meaning that given a sequence of couples <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx4.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[(m_{i},r_{i})]_{i=1}^{n}" display="inline"><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup></math> that commits to a value <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx4.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math>, it should be computationally infeasible for a PPT adversary to compute <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx4.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[(m_{i}^{\prime},r_{i}^{\prime})]_{i=1}^{n}" display="inline"><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup></math> such that <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx4.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[(m_{i}^{\prime},r_{i}^{\prime})]_{i=1}^{n}\neq[(m_{i},r_{i})]_{i=1}^{n}" display="inline"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mo>≠</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> also commits to <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx4.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math>.
The commitment scheme is also <span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">incremental</span>: let us consider a sequence <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx4.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[(m_{i},r_{i})]_{i=1}^{n}" display="inline"><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup></math>, its commitment <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx4.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math> and a couple <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx4.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(m^{\prime},r^{\prime})" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>m</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. Given the knowledge of <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx4.p1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c,m^{\prime}" display="inline"><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>m</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></mrow></math> and <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx4.p1.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r^{\prime}" display="inline"><msup><mi>r</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></math>, it is possible to compute <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx4.p1.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c^{\prime}" display="inline"><msup><mi>c</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></math> that commits to <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.P0.SPx4.p1.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[(m_{1},r_{1}),(m_{2},r2),...,(m_{n},r_{n}),(m^{\prime},r^{\prime})]" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>m</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></math>:</p>
<ul id="S3.I4" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S3.I4.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="S3.I4.i1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\blacksquare" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="normal">■</mi></math></span> 
<div id="S3.I4.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p"><math id="S3.I4.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathsf{COM}([(m_{i},r_{i})]_{i=1}^{n})\rightarrow c" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>𝖢𝖮𝖬</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> takes as input a sequence of messages and randomness and returns the corresponding commitment. <math id="S3.I4.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathsf{COM}" display="inline"><mi>𝖢𝖮𝖬</mi></math> is hiding and binding.</p>
</div>
</li>
<li id="S3.I4.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="S3.I4.i2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\blacksquare" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="normal">■</mi></math></span> 
<div id="S3.I4.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p"><math id="S3.I4.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathsf{INCR}(c,m^{\prime},r^{\prime})\rightarrow c^{\prime}" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>𝖨𝖭𝖢𝖱</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>m</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>c</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></mrow></math> takes as input a commitment <math id="S3.I4.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math> of a sequence <math id="S3.I4.i2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[(m_{i},r_{i})]_{i=1}^{n}" display="inline"><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup></math>, a new message <math id="S3.I4.i2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m^{\prime}" display="inline"><msup><mi>m</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></math> and a randomness <math id="S3.I4.i2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r^{\prime}" display="inline"><msup><mi>r</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></math>.
