<section id="S7.SS2.SSS0.P0.SPx2" class="ltx_subparagraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subparagraph">Latency test and transaction throughput.</h4>

<div id="S7.SS2.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Apart from Zcash, which is already deployed in real-world use, the only payment systems in the related work to report on their latency and throughput are Zef <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite> and UTT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>]</cite>.
The performance analyses of UTT and Zef were performed on different types of AWS EC2 instances (c5.4xlarge for UTT and m5.8xlarge for Zef).
Since the micro-benchmarks show better performance for PaxPay on UTT’s EC2 instance than on the one used by Zef, we chose to use the same instance type as in the Zef paper for consistency. <span id="footnote8" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">8</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">8</sup><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">8</span>We were unable to build and test the UTT code due to dependencies that broke over time. Since the UTT authors chose an EC2 instance type on which PaxPay performs better compared to the m5.8xlarge instance, we consider the results reported in the UTT paper to be suitable for direct comparison.</span></span></span></p>
</div>
<div id="S7.SS2.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">We thus run our PaxPay implementation on multiple m5.8xlarge instances, assigning one validator per instance.
For each version of PaxPay (regulated and non-regulated), we conducted two tests:
one with each validator running on a single CPU core, and another with each validator using <math id="S7.SS2.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="16" display="inline"><mn>16</mn></math> CPU cores.
The results are presented in Figures <a href="#S7.F2.sf1" title="Figure 2(a) ‣ Figure 2 ‣ Latency test and transaction throughput. ‣ 7.2 Performance analysis ‣ 7 PaxPay implementation and performance ‣ Fast, Private and Regulated Payments in Asynchronous Networks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2(a)</span></a> and <a href="#S7.F2.sf2" title="Figure 2(b) ‣ Figure 2 ‣ Latency test and transaction throughput. ‣ 7.2 Performance analysis ‣ 7 PaxPay implementation and performance ‣ Fast, Private and Regulated Payments in Asynchronous Networks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2(b)</span></a>.
We consider that the system support a given throughput if the corresponding transaction latency is smaller than 500 ms.
Our regulated implementation achieves the throughput of <math id="S7.SS2.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="100" display="inline"><mn>100</mn></math><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> tx/s</span> (transactions per second) in the single-core setup and <math id="S7.SS2.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="925" display="inline"><mn>925</mn></math><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> tx/s</span> in the 16-core setup.
Under the same conditions, Zef processes <math id="S7.SS2.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5" display="inline"><mn>5</mn></math><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> tx/s</span> and <math id="S7.SS2.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="88" display="inline"><mn>88</mn></math><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> tx/s</span>, respectively.
UTT processes <math id="S7.SS2.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="235" display="inline"><mn>235</mn></math><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> tx/s</span> using 16 cores.<span id="footnote9" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">9</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">9</sup><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">9</span>As stated in Zef <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>, each authority is distributed over multiple shards, each running in a single core.
The 16-core result is extrapolated from the linear relationship between throughput and the number of shards per validator, as shown in their paper.</span></span></span>
For the non-regulated PaxPay implementation, the throughput reaches <math id="S7.SS2.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="115" display="inline"><mn>115</mn></math><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> tx/s</span> in the single-core setup and <math id="S7.SS2.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1200" display="inline"><mn>1200</mn></math><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> tx/s</span> in the 16-core setup.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.SS2.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">These promising results can be attributed to the low verification time of the SNARK presented in the full version of the paper.
In the reference setting (regulated implementation with 1-core validators), the verification of the SNARK takes <math id="S7.SS2.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="9" display="inline"><mn>9</mn></math><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> ms</span> in our implementation while it takes <math id="S7.SS2.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="142" display="inline"><mn>142</mn></math><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> ms</span> in Zef with the same setting <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.SS2.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">The difference in performance between the regulated and non-regulated versions is due to the additional public parameters in the regulated SNARK.
This requires validators to perform more point multiplications on the elliptic curve used in the Groth16 construction.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.SS2.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">To improve scalability, validators can be <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">sharded</em> (run on multiple parallel machines) as in Zef and UTT.
The same approach could be applied to our system, though it has not been implemented.
A load balancer could efficiently distribute transfer requests among the validators by assigning a specific range of serial numbers to each shard of a validator. Upon receiving a request, the load balancer would determine the appropriate shard to handle it based on these predefined ranges.
Our experiments thus show that PaxPay is scalable.
The throughput can be improved even further by allocating more computational power to the validators, either by using more CPU cores per validator or by distributing the workload across additional machines.</p>
</div>

<section id="S8" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">8 </span>Discussion and comparison with related protocols</h2>

<section id="S8.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1" class="ltx_subparagraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subparagraph">Comparative analysis.</h4>

<div id="S8.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S1.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Summary. ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Fast, Private and Regulated Payments in Asynchronous Networks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> provides a comparison between PaxPay and the related protocols.
Lelantus appears to outperform Monero across all metrics in the table and offers larger anonymity sets.
We therefore decided to omit Monero from the table.
Similarly, Platypus was not included in the table, as we focus exclusively on decentralized payment systems.
Details and explanations regarding the data presented in the table can be found in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S8.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2" class="ltx_subparagraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subparagraph">Privacy.</h4>

<div id="S8.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">As shown in Table <a href="#S1.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Summary. ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Fast, Private and Regulated Payments in Asynchronous Networks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, PaxPay provides the strongest privacy guarantees, comparable to those provided by Zcash, whereas some protocols offer reduced privacy guarantees. This is especially the case for Zef and PRCash.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">To ensure full privacy, it is important to hide coin details when creating them with blind signatures. Yet, when the signatures are verified by validators, some users may still learn information on the payment.<span id="footnote10" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">10</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">10</sup><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">10</span>Suppose that, as in Zef <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>, we resort to only using blind signatures.
Let a user <math id="footnote10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math> creates a coin <span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">c</span> for a user <math id="footnote10.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math> during a transfer <math id="footnote10.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o_{1}" display="inline"><msub><mi>o</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>.
<math id="footnote10.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math> requests the validators to sign the blinded coin <math id="footnote10.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\mathbf{c}}" display="inline"><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐜</mi><mo>~</mo></mover></math>, and then sends the aggregated signature to <math id="footnote10.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>.
<math id="footnote10.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math> now spends <math id="footnote10.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{c}" display="inline"><mi>𝐜</mi></math> during a transfer <math id="footnote10.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o_{2}" display="inline"><msub><mi>o</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>, and in process
reveals <math id="footnote10.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{c}" display="inline"><mi>𝐜</mi></math> and the (randomized) signature.
Even though validators cannot reveal that the coin spent in <math id="footnote10.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o_{2}" display="inline"><msub><mi>o</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> was created in <math id="footnote10.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o_{1}" display="inline"><msub><mi>o</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>,
<math id="footnote10.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math> knows <math id="footnote10.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{c}" display="inline"><mi>𝐜</mi></math> and, thus, can deduce the sender of <math id="footnote10.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o_{2}" display="inline"><msub><mi>o</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> and a lower bound on the amount spent during <math id="footnote10.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o_{2}" display="inline"><msub><mi>o</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>.
</span></span></span>
UTT circumvents this problem by using a re-randomizable signature scheme (where both the signature and the signed message can be randomized), but this solution increases the workload for verifying transactions. Our solution is to verify the signature within the NIZK, which also decreases the validators workload.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S8.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx3" class="ltx_subparagraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subparagraph">Model assumptions.</h4>

<div id="S8.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">PaxPay is responsive, meaning it can be implemented in an asynchronous network.
Among the related protocols only Zef, UTT, and PARScoin also provide responsiveness. All the four protocols are built on some form of Byzantine consistent broadcast.
However, PARScoin requires correct validators (those who follow the protocol) to be honest, ensuring they do not share any information with the adversary.
In contrast, PaxPay tolerates correct validators being semi-honest, meaning they can share any information they receive or transmit during the protocol’s execution without compromising the system’s privacy guarantees.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S8.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx4" class="ltx_subparagraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subparagraph">Regulation.</h4>

<div id="S8.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">As displayed in Table <a href="#S1.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Summary. ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Fast, Private and Regulated Payments in Asynchronous Networks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>,
PaxPay does not support the <span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Limited held amount per user</span> feature.
PEReDi <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>]</cite> implements this feature, requiring synchrony between sender and receiver.
PARScoin <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite> claims a different approach: the sender initiates a transaction to reduce their balance, and the receiver can asynchronously claim funds later, provided their balance remains within the imposed limit.
However, this method merely limits the amount a user can hold at a given time, as receivers can bypass it by spending excess funds before claiming the pending funds they have received.
In practice, this mechanism has the same effect as setting a limit on the amount that can be spent in a single transaction.
We believe that implementing a <span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Limited held amount per user</span> feature is particularly challenging in a private and asynchronous payment system.
Such a feature would require that transfers atomically change the balances of both the sender and the receiver, to prove that receiver balance does not exceed a certain amount after executing the transfer.
However, to affect the balance of a user, privacy typically requires this user to interact with another user or the validators, in order to provide some secret data known only to him (such as coin data or account commitments).
Yet, asynchrony precludes live protocols from relying on interaction between senders and receivers.
Indeed, in an asynchronous setting, the sender who gets no response from the receiver cannot distinguish whether this absence of response is caused by network delays or by the receiver refusing to respond.
Implementing <span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Limited Held Amount per User</span> seems hard when ensuring both asynchrony and privacy.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">PaxPay also avoids <span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Full Asset Tracing</span> due to privacy risks.
Instead, it allows users to generate privacy-preserving proofs about their transactions.
Let us give a real life example. A user can prove that her account received funds from multiple addresses, each transfer being under a certain threshold, demonstrating legitimate income patterns.
This proof could demonstrate that the income pattern of a business is legitimate and consistent with regular business operations, precluding money laundering (which might involve receiving a large sum from a single address).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S8.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx5" class="ltx_subparagraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subparagraph">Performance.</h4>

<div id="S8.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">As mentioned in Section <a href="#S7.SS2" title="7.2 Performance analysis ‣ 7 PaxPay implementation and performance ‣ Fast, Private and Regulated Payments in Asynchronous Networks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7.2</span></a>, PaxPay outperforms all other protocols in terms of transaction throughput.
This performance advantage is directly attributed to its fast NIZK verification, which surpasses all existing protocols.
The only exception is Zcash, which also benefits from a fast NIZK verification but is constrained by the limitations of its underlying consensus protocol.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Additionally, the system’s scalability, that is achieved by increasing the computational power allocated to each validator, further strengthens its practical applicability.
The Visa payment system processed an average of <math id="S8.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="7,388" display="inline"><mrow><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>388</mn></mrow></math> transactions per second in 2024 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>]</cite>, which could be supported by PaxPay by distributing each validator across 8 m5.8xlarge EC2 instances each<span id="footnote11" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">11</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">11</sup><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">11</span>This estimation assumes a direct linear relationship between throughput and the computational power of the validators, as shown in Zef <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>.</span></span></span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">As mentioned in Section <a href="#S7.SS2" title="7.2 Performance analysis ‣ 7 PaxPay implementation and performance ‣ Fast, Private and Regulated Payments in Asynchronous Networks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7.2</span></a>, this high throughput comes at the cost of a relatively slow transfer proving, requiring between <math id="S8.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx5.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2" display="inline"><mn>2</mn></math> and <math id="S8.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx5.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="7" display="inline"><mn>7</mn></math> seconds depending on the user computational power to prove a transaction.
We believe that this delay is acceptable from the user’s perspective, especially since multiple payments can be aggregated into a single transfer.
As a result, even if a user needs to make numerous payments, she can prove them all within a single transaction, requiring only one proof.
It is worth noting that the statement being proven in such a case would be larger than for a proof of a single payment, which would still increase the proving time, though less significantly compared to generating a separate proof for each payment.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S8.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx6" class="ltx_subparagraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subparagraph">Use cases.</h4>

<div id="S8.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Our system is versatile and adaptable to various use cases. It can function as a standalone payment system, a CBDC, or a scaling solution for an existing blockchain (a so-called Layer 2).
It can be enriched with a <span class="ltx_text ltx_font_sansserif">Mint</span> and <span class="ltx_text ltx_font_sansserif">Redeem</span> operations that user would call to put or retrieve money in/from the system.
Depending on the use case, <span class="ltx_text ltx_font_sansserif">Mint</span> can be equipped with a proof showing that the user has the right to mint a new coin.
For example, if PaxPay were used as a scaling solution for Bitcoin, the <span class="ltx_text ltx_font_sansserif">Mint</span> operation would take some SPV (Simplified payment verification) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite> as input to prove to the validators that some value has been locked on Bitcoin.
The implementation of the <span class="ltx_text ltx_font_sansserif">Mint</span> and <span class="ltx_text ltx_font_sansserif">Redeem</span> operations would vary depending on whether the system is deployed as a CBDC or as a Layer 2 solution for a blockchain.
The performance of PaxPay (Section <a href="#S7.SS2" title="7.2 Performance analysis ‣ 7 PaxPay implementation and performance ‣ Fast, Private and Regulated Payments in Asynchronous Networks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7.2</span></a>) and its scaling capacity are key factors that enable our system to effectively address these use cases.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S8.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx7" class="ltx_subparagraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subparagraph">Bad user behavior.</h4>

<div id="S8.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">If a user tries to pass two transactions spending the same input coin, her account might get blocked because she will not get enough signatures for either of the transactions.
In this case, consensus is required to unlock the user’s account <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>, <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S8.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx8" class="ltx_subparagraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subparagraph">Future work.</h4>

<div id="S8.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Our protocol can be reused with some slight modifications to implement the same functionalities as in Zexe <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite>, hence not only offering a payment system but <span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">private computation</span>.
We can also considerably improve performance of our system by introducing sharding in the implementation, or improve the usability by moving to a different type of NIZK with a universal trusted setup.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S9" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">9 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S9.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">In this paper, we consider the problem of fully-private asset transfer (FPAT).
We propose PaxPay, an asynchronous FPAT protocol, prove its correctness, detail its implementation in Golang, and analyze its performance.
PaxPay leverages succinct non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs and threshold blind signatures.
Our system demonstrates significant improvements over existing systems, processing transactions at a high rate, while maintaining full anonymity for the users and responsiveness.
PaxPay also ensures regulatory enforcement, including some features that no other private payment system has managed to provide so far.
The flexibility offered by succinct NIZKs opens avenues for incorporating other regulatory compliance features with minimal impact on the system’s performance.
These elements make PaxPay suitable for a wide range of applications, from a scaling solution of blockchain to a standalone private payment system that can be used as a technical layer for CBDCs.</p>
</div>
</section>
